id: Body of Rags, International Bridge Between the US & Mexico

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Is it alive? —neither a head, legs nor arms! ................... ... torpid against the flange of the supporting girder . ? an inhuman shapelessness, knees hugged tight up into the belly Egg-shaped! —William Carlos Williams, 1950 visit to El Paso, from “Desert Music” Yes, I am a body of rags lying here on the bridge waiting for a hot rain to wash me open, dissolve me off the bridge because this border is closed. I rot on the boundary line and can’t enter Juarez, pennies thrown at me when a drunk El Pasoan returns in the darkness and sees my shape that makes him hurry across. No head, decades ago they threw it in the river without my screams. My arms were the first to go when I couldn’t climb the wall. I can never leave this bridge. I live on the pure line that divides countries and grabs my hunger from sliding into Mexico with my outstretched hands. I still have my knees. I used to be sold in Juarez and smuggled into El Paso, the egg that floated down the Rio Grande to break hundreds of miles away before being thrown back. I stay on the bridge and can’t move. Do not cross to El Paso without wiping your shoes of me, one foot on US concrete, the other scraping away at my Mexican rags. When I struggle against the wire fence, I make sure I salute two flags.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker depicts themselves as a shapeless, decaying body trapped on a bridge at the closed border between El Paso and Juarez.
- The poem presents the border as a violent boundary that prevents movement, fragments the body, and intensifies hunger.
- The speaker’s lost head and arms symbolize past violence, failed escape, and the physical cost of crossing or being denied passage.
- Images of being sold, smuggled, and thrown back evoke cycles of exploitation and forced displacement across the Rio Grande.
- The final image of saluting two flags while struggling against the fence highlights the speaker’s divided identity and captivity between nations.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The text explores the dehumanizing violence of the U.S.–Mexico border through a surreal, first-person persona of a dismembered body trapped on a bridge. It reveals the border as a site that erases identity, mobility, and humanity, making the speaker’s mutilated body a symbol of political exclusion and migrant suffering.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Egg, William, Carlos

outputs.L1:
“Is it alive? — neither a head, legs nor arms!  
...................  
... torpid against the flange  
of the supporting girder . ?  
an inhuman shapelessness,  
knees hugged tight up into  
the belly Egg-shaped!”  

—William Carlos Williams, 1950 visit to El Paso, from “Desert Music”  

Yes, I am a body of rags lying here on the bridge, waiting for a hot rain to wash me open, to dissolve me off the bridge, because this border is closed. I rot on the boundary line and cannot enter Juárez, while pennies are thrown at me when a drunken El Pasoan returns in the darkness and sees my shape—one that makes him hurry across.  

No head: decades ago, they threw it into the river without my screams. My arms were the first to go when I could not climb the wall. I can never leave this bridge. I live on the pure line that divides countries, the line that seizes my hunger and keeps it from sliding into Mexico with my outstretched hands.  

I still have my knees. I used to be sold in Juárez and smuggled into El Paso, the egg that floated down the Rio Grande only to break hundreds of miles away before being thrown back. I remain on the bridge, unable to move.  

Do not cross to El Paso without wiping your shoes of me: one foot on U.S. concrete, the other scraping away at my Mexican rags. When I struggle against the wire fence, I make sure to salute two flags.
outputs.L2:
Is it living? No head, no arms, no legs—only a numb mass pressed against the lip of the bridge’s steel support. A form not quite human, without clear shape, its knees drawn hard into its stomach. Like an egg.

—William Carlos Williams, during a 1950 visit to El Paso, from “Desert Music”

Yes, I am nothing but a ragged body stretched out on this bridge, waiting for a scorching rain to split me apart, to melt me away from the crossing, since the border will not open. I decay exactly on the dividing line, unable to pass into Juárez. Drunken men from El Paso, coming back through the dark, toss coins at me when they notice my outline and rush past in fear. I have no head; years ago, they cast it into the river, and my cries went with it unheard. My arms disappeared first, lost when I failed to scale the wall.

I am trapped forever on this bridge. I exist on the precise line between nations, the line that keeps my hunger from slipping into Mexico through my reaching hands. My knees remain. Once, I was bought and sold in Juárez, carried secretly into El Paso, an egg drifting along the Rio Grande until it cracked hundreds of miles downstream and was flung back again.

Now I remain on the bridge, motionless. If you cross into El Paso, do not do so without cleaning me from your shoes: one foot planted on American concrete, the other grinding my Mexican tatters away. And when I strain against the wire barrier, I make certain to honor both flags.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents its speaker as a shapeless, decaying body trapped on a bridge at the closed border between El Paso and Juárez. This setting is significant because the bridge should represent passage, connection, and movement between two places. Instead, it becomes a site of imprisonment. The speaker is suspended between nations, unable to move forward or return freely. Their body is described as damaged and incomplete, suggesting not only physical suffering but also the loss of identity and human dignity caused by border violence.

The border is portrayed as a violent boundary rather than a simple political line. It blocks movement, separates people from safety or opportunity, and transforms the speaker’s body into something fragmented and wounded. Hunger is also intensified by this confinement. The speaker’s inability to cross means they remain trapped in a state of deprivation, exposed to both physical need and political abandonment. The border does not merely divide land; it actively harms those who are forced to confront it.

The speaker’s missing head and arms carry symbolic meaning. The lost head may suggest erased identity, silenced memory, or the trauma of past violence. Without a head, the speaker is denied a full selfhood and a clear voice. The missing arms can represent failed attempts to escape, work, reach out, or defend oneself. Together, these absent body parts emphasize the physical cost of migration and the brutality faced by those who try to cross or are denied passage. The body becomes evidence of the violence produced by the border.

The poem also uses images of being sold, smuggled, and thrown back to evoke cycles of exploitation and forced displacement across the Rio Grande. These images suggest that migrants are treated as objects rather than human beings. They are moved, traded, used, and discarded by systems of power, smugglers, and border authorities. The repeated motion across the river does not lead to freedom; instead, it becomes a cycle of hope, rejection, and return. The Rio Grande, often imagined as a natural boundary, becomes part of a larger system that traps vulnerable people in repeated suffering.

In the final image, the speaker salutes two flags while struggling against the fence. This moment powerfully captures the speaker’s divided identity and captivity between nations. Saluting both flags suggests a forced loyalty to two countries, or perhaps an inability to belong fully to either one. At the same time, the speaker’s struggle against the fence shows that national symbols offer no real freedom or protection. The speaker remains caught between borders, identities, and political powers. The poem ultimately portrays the border as a place where the human body is broken, identity is divided, and movement becomes a painful struggle for survival.
outputs.L4:
The text presents the U.S.–Mexico border as a place of extreme violence, fragmentation, and dehumanization. Through a surreal first-person voice, the speaker appears as a dismembered body trapped on a bridge, unable to move forward or return. This disturbing image transforms the border from a simple geographic boundary into a brutal political space where bodies are controlled, identities are stripped away, and human beings are reduced to suffering flesh.

The speaker’s fragmented body becomes a powerful symbol of the migrant experience. Being dismembered suggests not only physical violence but also the emotional and social destruction caused by borders, policing, and exclusion. The body is no longer whole, just as the speaker’s identity is no longer fully recognized. Instead of being seen as a person with a history, desires, and rights, the speaker is treated as an object caught between nations. The bridge, which should represent passage or connection, becomes a place of suspension and entrapment.

By using surreal imagery, the text emphasizes how unnatural and inhumane the border system is. The speaker’s condition may seem impossible or dreamlike, but it reflects real forms of suffering experienced by migrants: separation from family, loss of dignity, fear of violence, and the denial of movement. The mutilated body exposes the cruelty hidden beneath political language about security, citizenship, and national boundaries.

Ultimately, the text argues that the border does not merely divide land; it divides people from their humanity. It turns migration into a state of pain and uncertainty, where the body itself becomes evidence of political exclusion. The speaker’s dismemberment represents the broader suffering of migrants whose lives are interrupted, controlled, or destroyed by the border. Through this haunting persona, the text forces readers to confront the human cost of a system that treats certain bodies as disposable.
outputs.L5:
William Carlos looked at the small white egg on the kitchen table as if it were a secret waiting to be opened. It was simple, smooth, and quiet, yet it seemed to hold an entire world inside its shell.

“An egg is more than breakfast,” he said with a smile. “It is a beginning.”

He thought of William Carlos Williams, the poet who found beauty in ordinary things: a red wheelbarrow, plums in an icebox, rainwater, and chickens. Perhaps, Carlos imagined, the egg could become a poem too—plain at first glance, but full of life, warmth, and possibility.

So he picked up a pencil and wrote:

A single egg  
rests in morning light—  
the world, unbroken.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in the voice of the “inhuman shapelessness” William Carlos Williams describes in “Desert Music” during his 1950 visit to El Paso, placing the figure on the El Paso–Juárez border bridge and exploring bodily fragmentation, migration, and the violence of the boundary line.
counterfactuals.output:
I stand where the bridge makes a sentence of the river and then cuts it in two.

I have no passport because I have no face to staple to its blue page. No mouth the officer can compare to a photograph, no eyes to lower, no hands except the hands I borrow from those who grip their papers until the papers soften with sweat. I am the loosened outline of everyone halted here: shoulder, bundle, heel, infant skull, plastic bag, scar under a sleeve. I am the body before it is counted, after it is searched. I am the name rubbed thin by dust and waiting.

Below me the river goes on being less than a river, a ribbon of refusal, a wet wire. Men have named it boundary, as if water could learn obedience. They have driven steel into the bank, poured concrete into the throat of the land, hung flags above the crossing like bandages over an unclosed wound. The line says: here the foot becomes foreign. Here the mother becomes suspect. Here hunger must explain itself. Here the body is divided into lawful and unlawful parts.

My left side is El Paso: hospital light, courthouse stone, desert brightness striking windshields. My right side is Juárez: exhaust, altar flowers, roofs patched with tin, music broken open in the street. But I am not left or right. I am the torn seam between them. I am what leaks through.

At noon the heat enters me and finds no center. I scatter into elbows in a queue, into a tongue translating fear, into the coin-bright gaze of a child watching uniforms. A grandmother’s knees tremble and I tremble there. A young man’s back remembers a train, a field, a night of running, and I lengthen along his spine. In the booth, a stamp descends with the sound of a small door closing inside the chest.

Do not ask what country made me. I was made by the cut. By the river taught to accuse. By the bridge that promises passage and practices refusal. By the map’s black vein, by the rifle’s patience, by the question repeated until even the innocent forget their answers.

Still, I move. Shapeless, yes—but not empty. I carry the fragments that borders create and deny: the foot blistered past geography, the breast drying for a child left behind, the throat full of unsent names, the hand reaching through mesh for another hand. I am inhuman only because the human has been broken here into documents, permissions, shadows.

When evening comes, the bridge glows like a bone held over flame. People cross, are turned back, cross again in memory, cross in rumor, cross in dreams with their bodies made whole by walking. I gather what falls from them: lint, breath, prayer, the dust of two cities grinding together.

And in the dark, under the flags, above the river, I become enormous—not a monster, but the shape of what no nation can admit it has made.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark ekphrastic monologue responding to this quotation: “Is it alive? —neither a head, legs nor arms! ... torpid against the flange of the supporting girder . ? an inhuman shapelessness, knees hugged tight up into the belly Egg-shaped!” Make it surreal, political, and set at the U.S.–Mexico border.
counterfactuals.output:
Is it alive?

The patrolman asks the question the way a museum guard asks you not to touch the glass.  
Not with curiosity—  
with the bored authority of a nation that has already decided what counts as flesh.

There, under the bridge, where the steel ribs of the border hum with heat,  
something is curled against the girder:  
not a body, not yet a body, not legally a body,  
only a knot of shadow clinging to infrastructure.  
A black egg laid by history.  
A seed of hunger.  
A saint with no face.  

No head, no arms, no legs—  
because the state has itemized them elsewhere:  
hands in the lettuce fields, backs in the kitchens, feet in the desert,  
names in detention databases, children in foil blankets,  
tongues cut into two languages and called evidence.

Look closer.  
The shape is not shapeless.  
It is the exact shape of someone trying to disappear  
inside the only architecture permitted to them:  
a crouch, a recoil, a prayer compressed into muscle.  
Knees hugged into belly, spine bowed like a question mark  
the empire refuses to read.  

Above it, the bridge carries trucks northward—  
avocados, televisions, auto parts, refrigerated meat—  
commerce passing freely over the place where a person cannot.  
The girders gleam with the dull theology of trade.  
Bolts, rivets, tariffs, visas, drones:  
all of it arranged with priestly precision  
around this small torpid egg of breath.

O border, you long metallic animal,  
you horizontal god fed by maps—  
what have you birthed beneath yourself?

The thing stirs.

Or perhaps the heat stirs around it.  
Perhaps the river remembers when it was not a wound.  
Perhaps the wall, in its sleep, dreams of being sand again.  
I see the shape pulse once,  
and every floodlight flinches.

Is it alive?

Ask the desert, whose mouth is full of bones.  
Ask the detention center vending machine glowing blue at midnight.  
Ask the judge on the screen, the child behind plexiglass,  
the mother reduced to a case number,  
the father swallowed by a workplace raid  
while his lunch went cold in the break room.  

Alive is not the question.

The question is:  
what kind of country needs a human being  
to become this small before it can look at them?  

Egg-shaped, yes—  
but not innocent.  
Nothing is innocent here.  
Even birth is political.  
Even sleep is trespass.  
Even the body, folded into itself beneath American steel,  
is accused of crossing.

And still, inside that dark oval,  
something gathers:  
not a monster, not a migrant, not an alien,  
but a future with its limbs withdrawn,  
waiting out the helicopters,  
waiting out the paperwork,  
waiting out the anthem and the rifle and the flag  
until the shell of fear cracks.

Then the shapelessness will unfold.

And those who called it inhuman  
will recognize, too late,  
the face they tried to erase  
was looking back from underneath the bridge all along.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental first-person poem from the perspective of a rag-like, headless body trapped on a bridge between El Paso and Juárez, using imagery of rot, flags, shoes, fences, the Rio Grande, and an impossible border crossing.
counterfactuals.output:
I was sewn badly to begin with—  
a slack country of sleeves,  
no head to hang a sky on,  
no mouth to stamp with yes / no /  
papers / water / wait.

On the bridge I wrinkle.

El Paso lifts its windows behind me,  
Juárez burns its little suns ahead,  
and between them I am inventory:  
rag-body, road-dust,  
one shoe tied to a rumor,  
one shoe missing its foot.

The flags above me slap and slap—  
bright wounds practicing wind.  
They do not rot, not visibly.  
They are taught to wave  
over everything that does.

Under the bridge, the Rio Grande  
drags its brown thread through the heat,  
stitching nothing to nothing.  
I would drink it if I had a face.  
I would drown if I had a name.

A fence grows from the dirt  
like metal grass, like teeth  
combing the horizon’s scalp.  
I press my fabric ribs against it.  
I snag. I tear. I become  
more border than body.

There are shoes everywhere—  
paired, unpaired, softened by sun,  
filled with silt, with ants,  
with the careful absence of people.  
They point north. They point south.  
They point into the river  
as if the river were a door  
that forgot how to open.

My stuffing smells sweet now.  
Rot has its own passport:  
green stamp, black stamp,  
flies signing in loops  
where my heart would have been.

I try to cross.

The officers ask for my face.  
I show them fray.  
They ask for my voice.  
I shake loose dust.  
They ask for my country.  
I unfold—  
El Paso in one sleeve,  
Juárez in the other,  
the bridge pinning me  
like laundry no one will claim.

Impossible, says the booth.  
Impossible, says the fence.  
Impossible, says the river,  
but it keeps moving.

So I cross by not crossing.

I leak cotton into the checkpoint.  
I shed threads into two nations.  
I let the wind smuggle me  
fiber by fiber,  
rag by rag,  
until I am everywhere caught—  
on barbed wire, on shoehooks,  
on the tongues of flags,  
in the Rio Grande’s brown mouth—

headless, yes,  
but listening  
with my whole torn body.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Using William Carlos Williams’s “Desert Music” as a springboard, write a lyrical prose piece about a deformed object or body lying on an international bridge, unable to enter either country, blending grotesque physical description with commentary on border enforcement.
counterfactuals.output:
At the midpoint of the bridge lay a thing no customs form could name.

It had once been a body, or a bundle, or a suitcase swollen by weather—something made for carrying. Now it had no clear front or back. Its seams had split in the sun. A blue-black heel protruded from one side like a bruised fruit. A hand, if it was a hand, opened from the other: five stiff petals, each nail packed with bridge dust. Its face had been rearranged by heat and waiting. The mouth, warped into an oval, seemed less an organ than an abandoned doorway. Flies entered and left with the confidence of officials.

Cars slowed, then accelerated.

The flags at either end performed their bright, obedient trembling.

No one knew which side had jurisdiction over the thing, because it lay exactly where the painted line crossed the road—one hip in one republic, one shoulder in another, the spine taking the border as if it were a bed. The guards conferred through radios. Their words clicked and traveled, returned clipped and metallic, never touching the object itself. Procedure required identification. Identification required possession. Possession required entry. Entry required permission. Permission required proof the thing was not what it appeared to be: a failure of categories, a ruined petition, flesh without a country.

The bridge, meanwhile, held it up.

Below, the river moved in its old brown language, carrying reeds, oil rainbows, plastic bottles, the moon’s thin coin. It had no booths, no turnstiles, no dogs trained to scent desperation. It crossed itself endlessly and was not arrested.

A woman in a car with children in the back seat covered their eyes too late. The children had already seen the foot, purple and enormous, its toes curled inward like questions refusing translation. They had seen the stomach caved and risen in wrong places, the shirt hardened with salt, the belt buckle shining at the center of the disaster as though still proud of its small authority. They had seen that the thing was not monstrous because it was inhuman, but because it had been left long enough for the human to become disputable.

On the north side, a man stamped passports under fluorescent light.

On the south side, another man lifted a gate and let commerce pass.

Between them, the object ripened in the impartial glare.

The bridge had been built to join two shores, but every bolt in it had learned division. Steel remembered the hands that placed it, hands with lunches wrapped in paper, hands that crossed home at dusk without being asked to prove their longing. Now cameras nested in its ribs. Sensors watched the heat signatures of mammals. Floodlights erased the stars. The bridge listened for names and found only engines.

The body—or the bundle, or the evidence—had no papers visible. Perhaps they had dissolved in sweat. Perhaps a wallet had been taken by the river, or by hunger, or by someone who knew that documents survive better than people. Perhaps there had never been papers, only a name carried in the mouth, and the mouth now was full of insects, full of the black music of refusing to close.

A vulture circled once, then thought better of international complications.

The officers placed orange cones around the thing, giving it at last a ceremony: a little crown of caution, a municipal halo. Traffic narrowed to one lane. Drivers leaned toward the windows to look, then looked away with the practiced shame of those who have been trained to confuse witnessing with trespass. The radios continued. The flags continued. The river continued.

By noon the heat had made the object eloquent.

Its skin spoke in blisters. Its cracked lips spoke in thirst. The twisted ankle spoke of walking after the road ended, after the bus fare ended, after the map became rumor. The back, bent almost double, spoke of crouching under wire, under freight, under the low ceiling of laws written by people who sleep indoors. One eye, sealed by swelling, accused no one. The other, half open, reflected the sky without allegiance.

And still the question was not: Who is this?

The question was: Where did it fall?

As if falling were a matter of policy. As if the last inch of collapse could assign blame. As if the body, in its final diplomacy, had not chosen the line deliberately—had not laid itself across the wound and become the wound’s visible grammar.

There it remained, refused by both nations and claimed by the sun.

Toward evening, a wind came from the desert, carrying sand so fine it seemed less like earth than memory ground down. It moved over the bridge and dusted the thing gently, filling the ear, the collar, the torn places in the shoe. For a moment the deformity softened. The body became a dune, a province, a map without ink. The cones glowed. The booths shone. The officers changed shifts.

Night opened its enormous passport and stamped everything dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a borderlands prose poem that begins with a quoted fragment from William Carlos Williams about an egg-shaped, limbless figure, then shifts into the figure’s own voice as it describes being smuggled, discarded, and eternally stuck between Mexico and the United States.
counterfactuals.output:
“an egg-shaped, limbless figure” — William Carlos Williams

I was packed in newspaper with the oranges, under the spare tire, inside the false bottom of a saint’s wooden chest, my shell knocking softly against the contraband rosaries. They told me to keep quiet, but what mouth could betray them? I had only my smoothness, my sealed little weather, my face imagined by whoever needed a face. In Sonora they called me mijo, in Arizona they called me evidence. At the checkpoint the dog sneezed and the agent lifted me into the white glare like a moon he did not recognize. Nobody knew whether to crack me open or pray.

Later, when I had no owner, I rolled from the ditch to the culvert, from the culvert to the dry wash, from the wash to the fence’s shadow. I learned the grammar of discarded things: water jugs gone opaque with sun, black backpacks split like beetles, baby shoes stiff with dust, IDs bitten by rain until every name became a blur. I lay among them, a citizen of aftermath. The helicopters wrote their angry circles above me. The vultures kept their patient court. At night the desert cooled its iron tongue and licked me clean.

I have been handed from coyote to cousin, from cousin to patrolman, from patrolman to inventory shelf, from shelf to forgetting. Each time I am named, I lose a border; each time I am lost, another line is drawn through me. Mexico dreams me as a seed that never sprouted. The United States files me as an object of unknown origin. Between them I remain: not born, not buried, not deported, not admitted.

Do not ask which side I belong to. I am the pause in the crossing, the held breath beneath the tarp, the white oval of fear in a mother’s throat. I am what rolls back when history pushes. I am small enough to hide in a hand, too large to disappear. I have no limbs, yet I have traveled farther than mercy. I have no mouth, yet I speak in the dust that coats both flags.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
